replacement: When Fyodor Pavlovitch heard how Smerdyakov was turning out, he made up his mind to have him as his cook, and sent him to Moscow to train. He stayed there some years and came back strikingly changed in looks. He seemed extraordinarily old for his age. His face had gone wrinkled and yellow, and strangely unmanly. In character he seemed almost exactly as he had been before leaving. He was as unsociable as ever and showed not the slightest wish for company. In Moscow, too, as we heard afterwards, he had always kept silent. Moscow itself had little interest for him; he saw very little of it and noticed hardly anything. He went to the theater once, and came back quiet and put out by it. On the other hand, he returned to us from Moscow well dressed, in a clean coat and clean linen. Every day, without fail, he brushed his clothes with great care twice, and he loved cleaning his smart calf boots with a special English polish until they shone like mirrors. He turned out to be a first-rate cook. Fyodor Pavlovitch paid him a salary, and Smerdyakov spent nearly all of it on clothes, pomade, perfume and the like. But he seemed to hold women in just as much contempt as men. With them he was discreet, almost unapproachable. Fyodor Pavlovitch began to see him a little differently. The fits were coming more often, and on the days when he was ill Marfa cooked, which did not suit Fyodor Pavlovitch at all.

“Think it over for yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch,” Smerdyakov went on, sedate and unruffled. He was aware of his triumph, yet, as it were, generous toward the beaten foe. “Think it over for yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch. The Scripture says that if you have faith as small as a mustard seed and tell a mountain to move into the sea, it will move at your word without the slightest delay. Very well, Grigory Vassilyevitch. I am without faith, and you have so great a faith that you swear at me constantly. So you try it. Tell this mountain to move, not into the sea, which is a long way off, but just into our stinking little river at the bottom of the garden. You will see for yourself that it will not budge. It will stay exactly where it is, however much you shout at it. That shows, Grigory Vassilyevitch, that you do not have faith in the proper manner, and only abuse other people about it. Consider this as well. In our day nobody, not only you but actually nobody, from the highest person to the lowest peasant, can push mountains into the sea—except perhaps one man in the whole world, or two at the most, and they are very likely saving their souls in secret somewhere in the Egyptian desert, so you would never find them. Now, if that is the case, and all the rest have no faith, will God curse all the rest? That is, the population of the entire earth, except for about two hermits in the desert? And in His well-known mercy, will He not forgive even one of them? And so I am convinced that although I may once have doubted, I shall be forgiven if I shed tears of repentance.”
